sourceBindings.text: A safety data sheet, or SDS, gives information about a chemical's hazards and safe handling. Before work, locate the relevant SDS and the site's response plan. First-aid measures, accidental-release measures, protective equipment and disposal information answer different questions. The trainer should help you find the relevant instructions rather than expecting you to guess from a product name.

Choose protection for the substance and task. In the liquid-fertilizer simulation, select the chemical-resistant gloves, splash goggles and apron specified on the scenario card, check them and put them on correctly before the hands-on part. Ordinary cloth gloves can absorb a liquid and hold it against the skin. A glove being called chemical-resistant does not establish that it suits every chemical.

Locate the designated spill kit and check that its absorbents, tools and waste container are suitable for the represented product. Sand, absorbent pads, granules and clay-based cat litter are examples, not interchangeable instructions for every substance. Use only a compatible material specified by the plan or product guidance. Do not improvise a neutralizing chemical.

Protection does not make an unsafe atmosphere safe. If the response would require specialist respiratory protection or training you do not have, withdraw and call the authorized responders. You are practising a limited spill response, not qualifying to enter a hazardous atmosphere.

sourceBindings.text: Control means preventing more material from escaping. For the authorized practice case, this means carefully returning the fallen container to an upright position. First check the scenario's hazards, warn others and confirm the required protection. Do not reach through the represented spill or put yourself where the container could splash you.

In a real incident, stopping a leak is conditional on the actual product, site plan, training and ability to do it safely. A damaged container, inaccessible valve or unknown reaction can make intervention unsafe. Do not handle a container simply because it is the first action in a memorized sequence.

If the leak cannot be stopped safely, tell the response lead and move to the safe area. Keeping people away and giving accurate information can be the most useful action you take. Do not let the wish to save equipment override the decision to withdraw.

sourceBindings.text: Containment limits where the liquid can travel. In the simulation, use the specified absorbent to make a barrier around the spill's perimeter. This raised barrier is sometimes called a dike. Explain where the liquid might flow before placing it, including any route towards a drain or watercourse.

Use the compatible absorbent identified in the scenario and follow the trainer's safe working sequence. The objective is to surround and contain the liquid while remaining outside the contaminated area. Do not walk through it or spread it with your footwear or tools.

Never hose a chemical spill into a drain or stream. That moves contamination somewhere else and can expose more people or the environment. If the release has already reached a drain or has spread beyond the planned response, report that fact immediately and do not pretend the small-spill exercise still applies.

sourceBindings.text: For the simulated liquid spill, apply the specified compatible absorbent to the contained liquid and allow it to take up the liquid. Collect the used material with the suitable scoop, dustpan or brush supplied for the exercise. Work carefully so that you do not splash or scatter it. Sweeping is not a universal method for all chemicals or powders.

Put the used absorbent, disposable pads, contaminated gloves and cleaning cloths into the designated compatible chemical-waste container for the represented product. Use the identification required by the plan. Keep incompatible wastes separate. A household rubbish bin or an unlabelled bag is not a substitute for the assigned disposal route.

The workbench exercise includes a final damp wipe. Do that step only because its scenario card says the represented product is compatible with that cleaning method. Collect the used cloth as chemical waste. Other products may need another cleanup method; follow the SDS and site instructions instead of applying the damp-cloth step automatically.

Remove or decontaminate protective equipment as trained, avoiding contact with the outside surfaces, and wash your hands thoroughly. Report the incident and any remaining contamination, used supplies or damage. The authorized person decides when the area can be used again. A surface looking clean does not by itself prove that it is safe.

sourceBindings.text: A wildfire or building fire, a major chemical release such as an ammonia leak, severe weather such as lightning or a tornado, or a threat of violence may require emergency movement. The correct destination depends on the hazard. Follow the site's emergency plan and the responsible coordinator: an outdoor assembly point suitable for a fire may be unsuitable during lightning, and some chemical incidents require shelter rather than crossing an exposed area.

Stop work when the alarm or instruction is given. Secure equipment only if that can be done safely without delaying escape. Leave by the designated safe route and follow instructions from the supervisor or emergency coordinator. Do not detour to retrieve tools, samples or personal belongings.

A muster point is a pre-agreed safe meeting place where the team can be accounted for. Think of an evacuation drill in which everyone goes to an agreed destination rather than scattering. Before fieldwork, identify your destination and the alternative route or destination to use if the first one is unsafe. Do not assume that the nearest open space is the correct place.

At the safe destination, check each person against the team's attendance information and report missing people immediately. Give the coordinator their names and last known locations if known. Do not re-enter to search on your own. Stay with the group unless directed otherwise, and do not return to work until the responsible authority gives permission.
